evidence.label: A power saving for intersective polynomial differences with an exponent depending only on the degree
A Power Saving for Polynomial Differences at Prime Arguments
A power saving for square-difference-free sets

headline: Sets of whole numbers with no square difference are smaller than N by a fixed power of N.
scope: The square result covers every N and every set in 1 to N. The polynomial and prime results cover fixed polynomials of degree at least 2, with constants depending on the polynomial.
plain: Pick numbers from 1 to N so that no two differ by a perfect square. Such a set must be a vanishing share of the numbers, but earlier bounds shrank that share only slowly. One paper proves the size is at most a constant times N to the power 1 − c, for a fixed tiny c. Two more papers claim similar savings for other polynomial differences and for prime inputs.
doesNot: This does not give a usable value for the exponent c, or close the gap with the best known constructions.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Hillel Furstenberg and András Sárközy, independently
scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers the fixed-power question of Green and Sawhney on a classical problem in additive combinatorics.

explanation:
Pick numbers from 1 to 20, but no two may differ by a perfect square: 1, 4, 9 or 16. How many can you take? One good choice is 1, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 16 and 18. These are the numbers that leave remainder 1 or 3 when divided by 5. Any difference between two of them leaves remainder 0, 2 or 3. A square never leaves remainder 2 or 3. A difference with remainder 0 would need to be at least 25 to be a square. So no difference is a square. A computer check confirms that 8 numbers is the most possible here.

The trick breaks at 26, because 26 − 1 = 25. Is there always some way to keep a fixed share of the numbers? No. In 1977 and 1978, Hillel Furstenberg and András Sárközy proved independently that the best share shrinks toward zero as the range grows[1]. A set with no square difference is called square-difference-free. The open question was how fast its share must shrink.

Sárközy's bound saved a small power of the logarithm of N, the top of the range[2]. A logarithm grows very slowly: the natural log of a billion is about 21. Later work sharpened this, including Bloom and Maynard in 2022[3]. In 2025, Ben Green and Mehtaab Sawhney proved a much stronger saving factor, about e to the power c√(log N)[4]. They asked whether a power saving holds. That means a bound of the form C times N to the power 1 − c, for fixed numbers c above zero and C[5].

From below, the record is far smaller. In 1984, Imre Ruzsa built square-difference-free sets of size about N to the power 0.733[6]. In 2026, Dmitry Krachun pushed the exponent just past 0.75[7]. A large gap remains between that and any upper bound[8].

This family has three papers. The first proves the power saving for squares[9,5]. The exponent c is a fixed number above zero, but extremely small[10]. The proof gives no useful value for it[11]. Even so, the shape matters. If c were 0.01, N to the power 0.99 would be ten times smaller than N once N has 100 digits. The gap keeps growing after that.

The second paper replaces squares with the values of other polynomials, h(1), h(2), h(3) and so on. Some polynomials can be dodged by a large set. Take h(x) = x² + 1. Its values 2, 5, 10, 17, 26 are never multiples of 3. So the multiples of 3 avoid every such difference, keeping a third of all numbers[12]. A polynomial is called intersective when, for every whole number q, some value of it is a multiple of q. This is exactly the condition needed for the share to shrink[13]. The value for each q may come from a different factor of h, and no whole-number root is needed[14].

For every intersective h of degree k at least 2, with a positive leading term, the second paper claims a power saving. The exponent depends only on the degree k[15]. The constant C may depend on every coefficient of h[16]. Before this, the best general saving was of the form e to the power (log N) to some fixed power below 1/2[17].

The third paper allows only prime inputs, so the forbidden differences are h(2), h(3), h(5), h(7) and so on. Here the needed condition is a little stronger. For each q, h must hit a multiple of q at an input sharing no factor with q. Under that condition, the paper claims a power saving[18]. One example is h(x) = (x − 1)². Forbidding only the differences (p − 1)², for primes p, already forces a power saving[19]. The best earlier bound, by Rice, saved only a power of log N[20]. In this paper the exponent may depend on h[21]. The proof also uses a result about the zeros of Dirichlet L-functions, functions that track primes in remainder classes. That result comes from a companion paper in the same release[22].

The main obstacle was that classical methods gain only slowly at each step. The new proof builds a quantity that is never negative. It is at least a fixed power of the density, the share of numbers in the set. It then shows this quantity shrinks by a power of N[23]. A key move zooms in on numbers spaced D² apart and relabels them as 1, 2, 3 and so on. A square difference in the relabeled set would give one in the original set[24]. For general polynomials, this zoom changes the polynomial, so the paper tracks a whole family of related polynomials[25].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the square result. It states that fixed constants c above zero and C work for every N. The polynomial and prime papers are not in the Lean scope note, so they remain claims. The prime paper also depends on the companion zero-free result. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean has checked a formal version of the square result. The polynomial and prime results are outside the Lean note. The prime result relies on a companion zero-free theorem, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A set of whole numbers where no two members differ by a perfect square such as 1, 4 or 9.
A bound of the form C times N to the power 1 − c, smaller than N by the growing factor N to the c.
A polynomial that, for every whole number q, takes some value that is a multiple of q.
The share of the numbers from 1 to N that belong to the set.
A function from number theory whose zeros control how primes spread among remainder classes.
A computer program that checks each step of a formally written proof.
